value.overview: The Eastern Kingbird (Tyrannus tyrannus) is a bold, widespread flycatcher of open country. It breeds across much of North America and migrates to Central and South America for the nonbreeding season. It is recognized by its dark upperparts, white-tipped black tail, pale underparts, and conspicuous white crown patch, usually hidden except during display or aggressive encounters. In Costa Rica, it occurs primarily as a migrant and winter visitor rather than a breeding species.
value.classification: The Eastern Kingbird belongs to the family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers, and the genus Tyrannus. Its scientific name is Tyrannus tyrannus.
value.identification: This medium-sized flycatcher has a charcoal-black head and back, white throat and underparts, and a dark tail with broad white outer edges. The wings are dark, and the bill is relatively short and broad. A small white or yellowish crown patch may be visible when the bird raises its feathers. Juveniles are browner and may show buff-edged feathers. It often perches upright on exposed twigs, wires, fences, or other prominent lookouts.
value.rangeHabitat: The Eastern Kingbird breeds from Alaska and Canada through much of the United States and locally in Mexico. It migrates through Central America and winters mainly in northern and central South America. In Costa Rica, it is found chiefly during migration and the boreal winter, especially from open lowlands and foothills, where it uses pastures, agricultural fields, savannas, forest edges, river margins, plantations, and lightly wooded areas. It generally avoids dense, closed forest.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Eastern Kingbirds pass through Costa Rica and commonly remain there during the nonbreeding season, with most records occurring roughly from September through April; they do not normally breed in the country.
value.breeding: Breeding occurs mainly in North America, not normally in Costa Rica. The species usually places a bulky open-cup nest on a horizontal branch, often near the edge of woodland, along a stream, or in a shelterbelt. The female generally lays two to five eggs, and both adults participate in caring for the young. Pairs defend nesting territories vigorously, frequently chasing crows, hawks, and other large birds from the vicinity of the nest.
value.dietFeeding: Eastern Kingbirds feed mainly on flying insects, including beetles, wasps, bees, grasshoppers, moths, and dragonflies. They usually hunt from an exposed perch, launching into the air to catch prey and returning to the same or a nearby lookout. During migration and winter, fruits and berries become an important part of the diet, particularly when insects are less abundant. The species may also forage over fields, water edges, and treetops.
value.behavior: This species is conspicuous and assertive. It often sits upright on exposed perches, makes short aerial sallies, and gives sharp calls while defending feeding or nesting areas. Eastern Kingbirds are strongly territorial during breeding and may attack much larger birds. Outside the breeding season they are less aggressive and may gather in loose groups, especially where fruit is plentiful. They migrate during the day and may travel in flocks during parts of the journey.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be declining, although the species remains widespread and relatively numerous.
conservation.threats: Potential concerns include loss and degradation of open woodland and grassland habitat, reduced food availability from intensive agriculture and pesticide use, collisions during migration, and habitat alteration on wintering grounds in Central and South America.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect varied open habitats with scattered trees, hedgerows, streamside vegetation, and native fruiting plants. Reduce unnecessary insecticide use, conserve migration and wintering habitats, and maintain bird-friendly agricultural landscapes. Supporting programs that monitor migratory birds can also improve knowledge of population changes and conservation needs.
